images.caption: Figure 1.Teaser ofSIA. A single reference pair(A,A′)(A,A^{\prime})may contain multiple edits at once. In this example, the changes include adding a logo, changing the expression, and replacing the background. Given a new query imageBB,SIAlets the user choose which edits to transfer. The same demonstration can produce different outputs, ranging from single-edit results to combinations of selected edits, while leaving the remaining edits out.

Figure 2.Overview of our selective image analogy pipeline. Given a demonstration pair(A,A′)(A,A^{\prime})containing multiple edits and a query imageBB, the model transfers only the user-selected edits to produceB′B^{\prime}. In this example,green textual tokensindicate retained edits that should be applied toBB, whilered textual tokensindicate suppressed edits that should not be transferred, even though they are present inA′A^{\prime}. The visual analogy guides the overall edit transfer, while the colored textual tokens specify which edits are retained or suppressed using selective token suppression and the Concept Suppression Vector (CSV).

Figure 3.Advantage of demonstration-based specification.Text conveys the category of an edit but not its exact form. In each row, the demonstration specifies the exact visual form of the edit, including its structure, shape, and color, which text-based editing fails to reproduce, while SIA matches the demonstrated transformation.

Figure 4.Visual comparison.Qualitative comparisons with existing approaches demonstrate that only our method can selectively suppress undesired edits while preserving the input image and applying the intended modifications. In contrast, other methods either apply all edits simultaneously (e.g., Relation Adapter) or substantially alter the input image, such as the dog introduced by LoRWeb.

Figure 5.Qualitative results.We provide multiple examples with different numbers of edits that can be switched to active or inactive. Our method is able to successfully control which edit needs to be applied.

Appendix DSIA vs Nano Banana qualitative comparison

images.caption: Figure 6.Visual comparison with Nano Banana.Qualitative comparisons against Nano Banana, a commercial multi-reference editor, show that onlySIAreproduces the demonstrated edit’s exact visual form. Nano Banana typically identifies the correctcategoryof edit, but fails to match the specific appearance shown inA′A^{\prime}: it renders sunglasses and the crown with the wrong shape, places the star logo in the wrong position, and produces an incorrect lipstick color. In contrast,SIAconsistently matches both the type and the precise form of each demonstrated edit while preserving the identity and structure ofBB.

Figure 7.Overview of our multi-edit dataset generation pipeline.For higher-order edit settings, we start from a base image and apply edits sequentially to obtain intermediate composites and the final full-edit image. For two-edit settings, we augment RelationAdapter pairs with an additional style transformation synthesized byFlux.2-Klein. All generated samples are filtered with Qwen2.5-VL to verify that the intended edits are correctly expressed.

Figure 8.Per-sample storage layout.Each leaf directory stores the source image, one reference image for each edit phrase, the sequence of composite images corresponding to retained subsetsℛ⊆ℰ\mathcal{R}\subseteq\mathcal{E}, and aprompt.jsonfile that maps every composite to a short natural-language description.

Figure 9.Visual ablation.Each row shows one demonstration pair(A,A′)(A,A^{\prime})and queryBB, with the four combinations ofExLoRAandCSVas columns (see the key at the top); the full method is boxed in green. The edits to retain (green) and to suppress (struck-through red) are listed on the right. Note that AnaLoRA is always active as it is needed to capture all the provided edits. All outputs areFlux.2-Klein results with anExLoRAtrained for only250250steps, on training-subject cases, withCSVas an additive push; the examples are selected (see text).

Figure 10.All edit combinations.For each demonstration pair(A,A′)(A,A^{\prime})and query imageBB, we show the output ofSIAfor every subset of the demonstrated edits, from a single retained edit to all of them. The chips under each output mark the selected (green) and excluded (red) edits.

Figure 11.Additional Results on portraits with multi-edit demonstrations.Each row shows SIA transferring a selected subset of the edits in a demonstration pair(A,A′)(A,A^{\prime})to a query imageBB. Green edits are retained and struck-through red edits are suppressed. The examples cover accessories, hair, expressions, backgrounds, and styles on portraits, from demonstrations with two to four edits.

Figure 12.Additional Results on portraits.Each row shows SIA transferring a selected subset of the edits in a demonstration pair(A,A′)(A,A^{\prime})to a query imageBB. Green edits are retained and struck-through red edits are suppressed. The examples cover expressions, accessories, poses, and backgrounds, mostly from two-edit demonstrations.

Figure 13.Additional Results on objects, scenes, and animals.Each row shows SIA transferring a selected subset of the edits in a demonstration pair(A,A′)(A,A^{\prime})to a query imageBB. Green edits are retained and struck-through red edits are suppressed. The examples cover candlelit-scene and pencil-sketch edits on fruit, a color change on a car, a color change on a dog, and wing and gold-color edits on a dragon.

Figure 14.Additional results with Qwen-Image-2.1.Each row shows SIA transferring a selected subset of the edits in a demonstration pair(A,A′)(A,A^{\prime})to a query imageBB. Green edits are retained and struck-through red edits are suppressed. The examples cover a carved texture on a fruit, armor with a new background, a beard, and hair color with a background. The beard row uses the same demonstration pair and query image as a row of Fig.12, for a side-by-side view of the two backbones. These are curated examples (Sec.I), and no baseline or user-study comparison exists for this backbone.

Figure 15.All edit combinations with Qwen-Image-2.1.For each demonstration pair(A,A′)(A,A^{\prime})and query imageBB, we show the output ofSIAfor every subset of the demonstrated edits: a crown, green hair, a Paris background and a Van Gogh style on a portrait (four edits), and a red T-shirt, a sitting pose and a painting style on a dog. The chips under each output mark the selected (green, tick) and excluded (red, cross) edits. All outputs are curated examples from the Qwen-Image-2.1 model of Sec.I, not fromFlux.2-Klein, and no baseline or user-study comparison exists for this backbone.

Figure 16.All edit combinations with Qwen-Image-2.1 (continued).More demonstrations in the format of Fig.15: sunglasses, a sad expression and a street background; armor, a beach hat and a kitchen background; and a bench, a red lamp light and an oil-painting style on a street scene.

Figure 17.All edit combinations with Qwen-Image-2.1 (continued).A crown, a gold necklace and an angry expression; and a beard, a surprised expression and a street background. These are curated examples from the Qwen-Image-2.1 model (Sec.I).
